title: Private key material served in a response
description: The response body carries a PEM private key block: the BEGIN/END markers and the base64 MII payload that follows them are the shape of an encoded key, not of sample text. A key served by a web endpoint is readable by anyone who can request the path, whatever algorithm it encodes.
remediation: Remove the file from the web root and rotate the key, because a served key must be treated as compromised. Store key material outside the document root and check for accidental inclusion in deployment artefacts.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the PEM markers and payload shape; it does not validate the key and cannot tell which service the key belongs to.
scopeT: One response whose body contains a PEM private-key block.
fp: A documentation page that quotes the BEGIN marker without a key body is not reported, because the base64 payload is required as well.
recordDesc: A PEM private key block is returned by the web endpoint, so the key material that block encodes is readable by whoever can request the URL.
applicability: Responses that serve files from a document root or an artefact store.
risk: Anyone who reads the key can impersonate the service, decrypt what it protects or sign as it does, and the key stays valid until it is rotated; HIGH because the secret is disclosed in full.
why: The body contains a PEM private-key BEGIN marker and a base64 MII payload.
fix: Remove the file from the web root.
Rotate the key, because it must be treated as disclosed.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm it no longer returns the key; confirm the replacement key lives outside the document root.

title: Terraform state file served
description: The response is a Terraform state document: the terraform_version and resources fields are the schema of the state file, which records every managed resource and, for many resource types, the attribute values that were applied.
remediation: Move the state to an encrypted remote backend with access control, treat this copy as disclosed, and rotate every credential the state contains. Add the state path to the deny list at the web server.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the state schema; it does not parse the stored attributes and cannot enumerate which secrets a particular state holds.
scopeT: One response whose body is a Terraform state document with terraform_version and resources fields.
fp: A hand-written JSON document that happens to use those two field names is reported as well; the fields together are the state schema.
recordDesc: A Terraform state file is served at this endpoint, so the applied infrastructure definition and any sensitive attribute values it stores are readable.
applicability: Responses served from a deployment directory or artefact store.
risk: State files commonly carry database passwords, private keys and access keys in plain text, and they map every managed resource for an attacker; HIGH because the file is a credential and architecture inventory in one.
why: The body is a Terraform state document with terraform_version and resources fields.
fix: Move the state to an encrypted remote backend.
Rotate every credential the state contains.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the state file is refused; confirm the backend is encrypted and access-controlled.

title: Database dump with schema statements served
description: The response is a database dump: the dump tool banner and a CREATE TABLE statement are the header and body of an exported schema with rows. A web server that serves it hands over the schema and the data in the same response.
remediation: Remove the dump from the web root and move exports to a private store with access control. Treat the data as disclosed and assess notification duties for the rows it contained.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the dump banner and a CREATE TABLE statement; it cannot count the rows or tell which tables the export covers.
scopeT: One response whose body carries a database dump banner and a CREATE TABLE statement.
fp: A tutorial page that quotes a dump banner and a table statement is reported too; the pairing is the export shape.
recordDesc: A database dump is served by the web endpoint, so table definitions and the rows the export contains are readable in one request.
applicability: Responses that serve files from a document root or a backup directory.
risk: The dump discloses table structure, column names and row data including personal and credential fields; HIGH because the export is the whole dataset rather than a sample.
why: The body carries a dump-tool banner and a CREATE TABLE statement.
fix: Remove the dump from the web root.
Move exports to a private store with access control.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the dump is refused; confirm exports live outside the document root.

title: Password file with hash records served
description: The response is an Apache htpasswd file: the user names and the `$apr1$` or `$2y$` hash prefixes are the record format of that file. It is a credential store, and the hashes are the only thing between a reader and the accounts.
remediation: Remove the file from the web root, move authentication data outside the document root, and rotate the passwords for every account listed.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the hash-record shape; it does not attempt to crack a hash and cannot tell which paths the file protects.
scopeT: One response whose body contains htpasswd-style records with apr1 or bcrypt hash prefixes.
fp: A page that documents the hash format with a single example line is reported as well; two or more record lines is the common shape.
recordDesc: An htpasswd file is served at this endpoint, so user names and the apr1 or bcrypt hashes that protect the listed accounts are readable and can be cracked offline.
applicability: Responses that serve files from a document root.
risk: An attacker who reads the file cracks the weak entries offline and reuses the user names against other services; MEDIUM because the hashes must be cracked before they are usable.
why: The body carries user records with $apr1$ or $2y$ hash prefixes.
fix: Remove the file from the web root.
Rotate the listed passwords.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the file is refused; confirm authentication data lives outside the document root.

title: AWS credentials file served
description: The response is an AWS shared-credentials file: the `[default]` or `[profile ...]` section header together with an aws_access_key_id key is the format the AWS CLI and SDKs read. The file pairs the access key id with its secret.
remediation: Remove the file from the web root, deactivate the exposed access keys, and issue replacements that are delivered through an instance role or a secret manager rather than a file.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the credentials-file shape; it does not use the key and cannot determine the permissions attached to it.
scopeT: One response whose body is an AWS shared-credentials file, identified by a profile section and an aws_access_key_id key.
fp: Documentation that shows the file format with placeholder values is reported too; the section header and key name are the format markers, so a served sample must not be reachable either.
recordDesc: An AWS shared-credentials file is served at this endpoint, so an access key id and its secret are readable together and can be used directly against the account.
applicability: Responses that serve files from a document root or a home directory.
risk: Anyone who reads the file uses the key pair directly against the account, with whatever permissions the key holds; HIGH because the pair is directly usable without cracking.
why: The body carries a credentials-file section header and an aws_access_key_id key.
fix: Remove the file from the web root.
Deactivate the exposed key pair and issue replacements.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the file is refused; confirm the keys are deactivated in the account.

title: Docker client configuration served
description: The response is a Docker client configuration file: the auths object keyed by registry URLs holds base64 user:password pairs for each registry. It is the file the Docker CLI reads from its configuration directory.
remediation: Remove the file from the web root, revoke the registry credentials it holds, and issue per-host tokens through a credential helper instead of a configuration file.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the configuration shape; it does not decode the auth values and cannot tell which registries are writable.
scopeT: One response whose body is a Docker client configuration with an auths object and a registry URL.
fp: A JSON document that names the auths key without registry URLs is not reported; the registry URL is required.
recordDesc: A Docker client configuration file is served at this endpoint, so registry credentials encoded in the auths object are readable.
applicability: Responses that serve files from a document root or a home directory.
risk: The decoded auth values authenticate to the registries they name, which lets a reader pull private images and push replacements; HIGH because registry write access is a supply-chain path.
why: The body contains an auths object with registry URLs.
fix: Remove the file from the web root.
Revoke the registry credentials and issue per-host tokens.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the file is refused; confirm the old registry tokens no longer authenticate.

title: Kubernetes kubeconfig served
description: The response is a Kubernetes kubeconfig: the clusters list with certificate-authority-data, and usually a user credential, is the document kubectl reads. A served kubeconfig carries both the API server address and the credential that authenticates to it.
remediation: Remove the file from the web root, revoke the embedded credential (delete the token secret or the client certificate), and issue short-lived credentials through a workload identity instead of a kubeconfig file.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the kubeconfig shape; it does not use the credential and cannot determine the role bound to it.
scopeT: One response whose body is a kubeconfig document with a clusters list and certificate-authority-data.
fp: A kubeconfig with no user credential is still reported, because the API server address and CA are disclosed as well.
recordDesc: A kubeconfig is served at this endpoint, so the cluster API address, its certificate authority and the client credential it embeds are readable in one request.
applicability: Responses that serve files from a document root or a CI artefact store.
risk: The embedded token or client certificate authenticates to the cluster with the permissions of the identity it represents, which is often cluster-admin for a deployment kubeconfig; HIGH because the credential is directly usable.
why: The body carries a clusters list with certificate-authority-data and a credential field.
fix: Remove the file from the web root.
Revoke the embedded credential and issue short-lived credentials.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the file is refused; confirm the old credential no longer authenticates.

title: npm authentication token file served
description: The response is an npm configuration file: the scope-qualified `_authToken` line together with a registry setting is the format npm reads for package-publishing credentials. The token is written in clear text.
remediation: Remove the file from the web root, revoke the token at the registry, and deliver registry credentials through CI secrets or a short-lived OIDC exchange rather than a committed file.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the token line and registry setting; it does not use the token and cannot determine its publish scope.
scopeT: One response whose body contains an _authToken assignment beside a registry setting.
fp: A .npmrc that only sets registry and save-exact is not reported; the token assignment is required.
recordDesc: An npm configuration file carrying an _authToken is served at this endpoint, so a package-registry publishing credential is readable in clear text.
applicability: Responses that serve files from a document root or a source archive.
risk: The token authenticates to the registry, which for a publisher scope allows publishing a package name the organisation owns; HIGH because a published package reaches every build that installs it.
why: The body carries an _authToken assignment and a registry setting.
fix: Remove the file from the web root.
Revoke the token at the registry.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the file is refused; confirm the token is revoked.

title: OpenAPI specification served
description: The response is an OpenAPI document: the openapi version field and the paths object list every documented operation, including any administrative or internal route the author left in.
remediation: Publish the description only to authenticated developers, and remove internal or administrative routes from the published subset. Where a public description is required, generate it without the internal operations.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the description document; it does not call the routes it lists and cannot show which of them authorize correctly.
scopeT: One response whose body is an OpenAPI 3 document with a paths object.
fp: An API that deliberately publishes its description is still reported; the finding is that internal operations are listed, which the reviewer must confirm.
recordDesc: The API description document is served at this endpoint, so the operation inventory is readable and maps endpoints that the rest of the site does not link.
applicability: Responses served by an API gateway or application server.
risk: The document names internal and administrative routes, parameter shapes and schemas, which shortens the path from browsing to targeting; LOW because a description is not an access grant.
why: The body is an OpenAPI document with an openapi 3 version field and a paths object.
fix: Restrict the description to authenticated developers.
Remove internal routes from the published subset.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the description is not served publicly, or no longer lists internal routes.

title: GraphQL IDE interface disclosed
description: The response is a GraphQL IDE shell: the GraphiQL or Playground container together with a graphql endpoint reference is the page a developer uses to run queries interactively. The IDE ships with a query editor pointed at the live endpoint.
remediation: Disable the IDE in production builds, or serve it only to authenticated developers behind a separate host. Keep introspection restricted to the audiences that need it.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the IDE shell; it does not run a query and cannot show whether introspection is enabled on the endpoint.
scopeT: One response whose body renders a GraphQL IDE shell.
fp: A documentation page that names GraphiQL is not reported; the IDE container element is required.
recordDesc: A GraphQL IDE is served at this endpoint, so an interactive query console against the GraphQL API is reachable and invites hand-written queries from any visitor.
applicability: Responses served by a GraphQL deployment.
risk: The IDE lets a visitor explore the schema and run queries by hand, which turns an introspection surface into a working console; MEDIUM because the API still authorises the queries it receives.
why: The body carries a GraphiQL or Playground container and a GraphQL endpoint reference.
fix: Disable the IDE in production.
Serve it only to authenticated developers.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the IDE is not served in production.

title: package.json manifest served from the web root
description: The response is a package.json manifest: the name, dependencies and version fields are the manifest schema, and they pin the exact package versions the application build resolved.
remediation: Serve the built application rather than its source manifest, and keep manifests outside the document root. Where a package identity is genuinely public, publish it from the registry instead.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the manifest; it does not look up any version against an advisory source and makes no claim that a pinned version is vulnerable.
scopeT: One response whose body is a package.json manifest with name and dependencies fields.
fp: A JavaScript bundle that contains the word dependencies but not the manifest fields is not reported.
recordDesc: A package.json manifest is served at this endpoint, so the dependency inventory and the exact versions the build resolved are readable without probing.
applicability: Responses served from a source directory or a misconfigured static root.
risk: Exact versions let a reader match the deployment against known issues for those releases without probing; LOW because the manifest alone is not an exploit and the packages may be patched by rebuilds.
why: The body is a package manifest with name and dependencies fields.
fix: Stop serving the manifest from the document root.
Publish package identity from the registry instead.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the manifest is not served.

title: ASP.NET web.config served with settings
description: The response is an ASP.NET configuration file: the configuration root, the system.webServer section and usually a connectionStrings block are the file schema. A served copy exposes connection strings and application keys in clear text.
remediation: Configure the server to refuse requests for configuration files, remove the file from the static root, and rotate every credential the file contains.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the configuration schema; it does not enumerate the values and cannot tell whether the credentials are still valid.
scopeT: One response whose body is an ASP.NET configuration document with a system.webServer section.
fp: A documentation page that quotes a configuration fragment is reported only when the full document shape appears.
recordDesc: An ASP.NET configuration file is served at this endpoint, so connection strings and application settings, which usually include credentials, are readable in clear text.
applicability: Responses served from an IIS or ASP.NET content root.
risk: A served configuration file hands over database credentials and API keys, and on IIS it is enough to reach the database directly; HIGH because the values are usable without cracking.
why: The body is an ASP.NET configuration document with a system.webServer section.
fix: Refuse requests for configuration files.
Rotate every credential the file contains.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the server refuses it; confirm the credentials were rotated.

title: Jenkins script console disclosed
description: The response is the Jenkins script console: the Groovy script editor and the Jenkins chrome identify the administrative page that runs arbitrary Groovy inside the controller process. The console is a remote-code-execution surface by design.
remediation: Require authentication and an administrative role for the script console, restrict Jenkins to the internal network, and confirm that anonymous read access is disabled.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the console page; it does not submit the form and cannot show whether the request was authorised.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the Jenkins script console.
fp: A documentation page describing the console is reported too when it carries the editor and the Jenkins chrome; the reviewer confirms which page it is.
recordDesc: The Jenkins script console is served at this endpoint, so the administrative Groovy console is reachable from this network position.
applicability: Responses served by a Jenkins controller.
risk: A caller who can submit the form runs code in the Jenkins controller with its credentials and access to every build secret; HIGH because the console is code execution by design once it is reachable and unauthenticated.
why: The body carries the Groovy script console and the Jenkins chrome.
fix: Require an administrator role for the console.
Restrict Jenkins to the internal network.
verifyT: Request the path without credentials and confirm the console is refused or redirects to login.

title: Jenkins dashboard disclosed
description: The response is the Jenkins dashboard: the Jenkins chrome together with the Manage Jenkins link and the job list identifies the controller home page. The dashboard names the jobs and exposes the management entry point.
remediation: Require authentication for the dashboard and disable anonymous read access. Restrict the controller to the internal network.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the dashboard; it does not open a job and cannot show whether builds or credentials are reachable.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the Jenkins dashboard with a management link.
fp: A login page that carries the Jenkins chrome but no job list is not reported.
recordDesc: The Jenkins dashboard is served at this endpoint, so the controller home page with its job list and management link is reachable.
applicability: Responses served by a Jenkins controller.
risk: Job names reveal deployment targets and repository layout, and an anonymous dashboard often accompanies anonymous build access; MEDIUM because the page is read-only.
why: The body carries the Jenkins chrome, the Manage Jenkins link and a job list.
fix: Require authentication for the dashboard.
Disable anonymous read access.
verifyT: Request the dashboard without credentials and confirm it redirects to login.

title: H2 database console disclosed
description: The response is the H2 console login form: the H2 Console heading together with the JDBC URL field identifies the embedded database console. The form accepts a JDBC URL, so the console itself decides which database to open.
remediation: Disable spring.h2.console.enabled outside development, and never expose the console on a network interface. If it is needed, bind it to loopback and require the database password.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the console form; it does not submit a JDBC URL and cannot show which databases the server can reach.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the H2 console login form.
fp: A page that describes the console without the JDBC URL field is not reported.
recordDesc: The H2 console is served at this endpoint, so an interactive SQL console that accepts a caller-supplied JDBC URL is reachable on the network.
applicability: Responses served by a Spring Boot application with the H2 console enabled.
risk: A reachable H2 console runs SQL against whatever database the submitted URL names, including remote databases the server can reach; MEDIUM because the console may still require a database password.
why: The body carries the H2 Console heading and a JDBC URL field.
fix: Disable the console outside development.
Bind it to loopback where it is needed.
verifyT: Request the console path and confirm it returns 404 in the deployed configuration.

title: Tomcat manager application disclosed
description: The response is the Tomcat manager application: the manager heading together with the Server Information block and the deploy form identifies the administrative console. That console deploys and undeploys web applications.
remediation: Remove the manager application from production, or restrict it to an administrative network with a manager role and a strong credential. Never publish /manager on the application ingress.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the manager page; it does not submit the deploy form and cannot show whether the request would be authorised.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the Tomcat manager console.
fp: A Tomcat error page is a different finding with its own rule and is not reported here.
recordDesc: The Tomcat manager console is served at this endpoint, so the deploy and undeploy controls are reachable from this network position.
applicability: Responses served by an Apache Tomcat installation with the manager webapp.
risk: A caller who can submit the deploy form installs a web application and runs code as the Tomcat user; HIGH because deployment is code execution once the console is reachable.
why: The body carries the Tomcat manager heading, the Server Information block and a deploy control.
fix: Remove the manager application from production.
Restrict it to an administrative network with a manager role.
verifyT: Request /manager/html and confirm it is refused or absent.

title: Adminer database console disclosed
description: The response is the Adminer login page: the Adminer product name together with the driver selector and the Log in control identifies the single-file database console. The form names the database engines the deployment supports.
remediation: Remove Adminer from production, or restrict it to the management network behind an authenticating proxy. Never leave the login page on the application ingress.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the login page; it does not attempt a login and cannot show which database privileges would follow.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the Adminer login form.
fp: A page that links to Adminer without the driver selector is not reported.
recordDesc: The Adminer console is served at this endpoint, so a database administration login that fronts the application database is reachable.
applicability: Responses served by an Adminer deployment.
risk: A reachable Adminer accepts credentials against the database and, after login, runs SQL and exports data; MEDIUM because the page is the login form and no session is established.
why: The body carries the Adminer product name, a driver selector and a login control.
fix: Remove Adminer from production.
Restrict it to the management network.
verifyT: Request the path and confirm the login page is not served.

title: Symfony profiler toolbar disclosed
description: The response carries the Symfony web profiler toolbar: the sf-toolbar element and the Symfony name are the toolbar that development builds inject into every page. The toolbar links a profiler that records queries, configuration and request data.
remediation: Disable the web profiler outside development (web_profiler toolbar false, debug false), clear the profiler store, and confirm the toolbar is absent from production pages.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the toolbar; it does not request a profile token and cannot show what a stored profile contains.
scopeT: One response whose body injects the Symfony profiler toolbar.
fp: A Symfony page without the toolbar is not reported; the toolbar element is required.
recordDesc: The Symfony profiler toolbar is present in the response, so the debug profiler is enabled on this deployment and its stored request profiles are likely reachable.
applicability: Responses rendered by a Symfony application.
risk: Profiler profiles record SQL, configuration values and request parameters, and are addressable by token; MEDIUM because the toolbar itself does not prove the profile store is reachable.
why: The body carries the sf-toolbar element and the Symfony name.
fix: Disable the web profiler outside development.
Confirm the toolbar is absent from production pages.
verifyT: Fetch a production page and confirm no sf-toolbar element is present.

title: Laravel Ignition error page disclosed
description: The response is the Laravel Ignition error page: the Ignition container together with the Laravel framework marker identifies the detailed exception renderer. That page shows stack frames, environment values and the source excerpt around the throw.
remediation: Set APP_DEBUG=false in production and confirm the generic error page is returned. Ignition should not be reachable on a production host.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the Ignition page; it does not read every rendered field and cannot show which environment values the page included.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the Ignition error page.
fp: The Laravel Whoops page is a different renderer with its own rule; a page carrying both markers is reported by both.
recordDesc: The Ignition error page is served, so the detailed exception renderer is enabled on this deployment and its diagnostics are visible to the caller.
applicability: Responses rendered by a Laravel application.
risk: The page discloses stack frames, file paths and often environment values, which is enough to plan a follow-up; MEDIUM because the diagnostic page itself does not execute code.
why: The body carries the Ignition container and the Laravel framework marker.
fix: Set APP_DEBUG=false in production.
Confirm the generic error page is returned.
verifyT: Trigger an error and confirm the response is the generic page without Ignition.

title: Traefik dashboard disclosed
description: The response is the Traefik dashboard: the Traefik name together with the dashboard container identifies the proxy administration UI. The dashboard lists routers, services and middlewares, including their forwarding targets.
remediation: Keep the dashboard on the internal network or disable it, and require authentication through a middleware when it must be reachable.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the dashboard; it does not read provider data and cannot show whether the API is enabled insecurely.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the Traefik dashboard.
fp: A page that mentions Traefik without the dashboard container is not reported.
recordDesc: The Traefik dashboard is served at this endpoint, so the proxy configuration view with its router and service inventory is reachable.
applicability: Responses served by a Traefik instance with the dashboard enabled.
risk: The dashboard maps every backend address and rule, which is a ready-made target list, and older releases exposed provider data without authentication; MEDIUM because the page is read-only.
why: The body carries the Traefik name and a dashboard container.
fix: Disable the dashboard or keep it internal.
Require authentication through a middleware.
verifyT: Request the dashboard and confirm it is not reachable from untrusted networks.

title: Prometheus Alertmanager UI disclosed
description: The response is the Alertmanager web UI: the product name together with the Alerts, Silences and Status navigation identifies the alert routing console. That console can create silences that stop pages from firing.
remediation: Require authentication in front of Alertmanager, keep it on the internal network, and alert on silence creation from unexpected sources.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the UI; it does not create a silence and cannot show whether the request would be accepted.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the Alertmanager console.
fp: The Prometheus metrics rule is a different product and a different page.
recordDesc: The Alertmanager UI is served at this endpoint, so the alert routing console and the silence controls that can suppress pages are reachable.
applicability: Responses served by an Alertmanager instance.
risk: A caller who can create a silence suppresses the alerts that would report an incident; MEDIUM because a silence requires the console to accept the request.
why: The body carries the Alertmanager name and the console navigation.
fix: Put authentication in front of Alertmanager.
Keep it on the internal network.
verifyT: Request the UI and confirm it is not reachable without authentication.

title: MinIO object-storage console disclosed
description: The response is the MinIO console: the MinIO product name together with the console shell identifies the object-storage administration UI. The console manages buckets, access keys and lifecycle rules.
remediation: Keep the console on the internal network behind an authenticating proxy and issue scoped service accounts instead of root credentials.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the console shell; it does not list a bucket and cannot show whether a login would succeed.
scopeT: One response whose body renders the MinIO console.
fp: The bucket-listing rule reports anonymous listings and is a different finding.
recordDesc: The MinIO console is served at this endpoint, so the object-storage administration interface, which manages buckets and access keys, is reachable.
applicability: Responses served by a MinIO deployment.
risk: A reachable console exposes the bucket inventory and, after login, access-key and policy management; MEDIUM because the page alone does not prove credentials are accepted.
why: The body carries the MinIO product name and a console shell.
fix: Keep the console on the internal network.
Issue scoped service accounts.
verifyT: Request the console and confirm it is not reachable from untrusted networks.

title: HashiCorp Vault UI disclosed
description: The response is the Vault web UI: the Vault name together with the seal-status panel identifies the secrets-engine console. The panel distinguishes a sealed from an unsealed instance and leads to the unseal flow.
remediation: Keep the Vault UI on the management network behind an authenticating proxy, and never expose the listener on the application ingress.

Keep core and plugins updated.

title: Obsolete Feature-Policy header present
description: The response sends `Feature-Policy`, the header that Permissions-Policy replaced. Current browsers ignore it, so a deployment that believes it restricted a powerful feature through this header has in fact declared nothing, and the two headers can disagree while both are present.
remediation: Move every directive to Permissions-Policy, which uses `feature=(allow-list)` syntax, and remove Feature-Policy once the translation is verified.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the obsolete header; it does not compare it with any Permissions-Policy that is also present and cannot say which features end up allowed.
scopeT: One response that carries a Feature-Policy header.
fp: A deployment that keeps Feature-Policy for an old client is still reported; current browsers ignore the header.
recordDesc: The Feature-Policy header is ignored by current browsers, so the restriction it declares is not applied and the deployment has no effective policy from this header.
applicability: Responses that send a security header.
risk: A powerful feature the deployment meant to block stays available to embedded frames; LOW because a Permissions-Policy may still be in force beside it.
why: The response carries a Feature-Policy header.
fix: Translate the directives to Permissions-Policy.
Remove Feature-Policy afterwards.
verifyT: Fetch the page and confirm Feature-Policy is gone and Permissions-Policy states the intended policy.

title: Removed Public-Key-Pins header present
description: The response sends `Public-Key-Pins`, a header that was removed from the specification after browsers stopped implementing it. It now adds bytes to every response and no protection, and a pinning mistake is not mitigated by anything the header claims.
remediation: Remove Public-Key-Pins and rely on HSTS plus certificate transparency monitoring. If pinning is required, implement it in the client rather than through a removed header.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the removed header; it does not evaluate the pin list and cannot say whether any client still honours it.
scopeT: One response that carries a Public-Key-Pins header.
fp: A prepared-but-unshipped configuration is not observable; the rule reports the header only when it is sent.
recordDesc: Public-Key-Pins no longer has any effect in browsers, so the pinning protection the deployment believes it configured does not exist.
applicability: Responses that send a security header.
risk: An operator may believe certificate pinning is enforced and skip other controls; LOW because the absence of protection is the whole impact.
why: The response carries a Public-Key-Pins header.
fix: Remove Public-Key-Pins.
Use HSTS and certificate transparency monitoring instead.
verifyT: Fetch the page and confirm the header is absent.

title: Obsolete X-XSS-Protection auditor enabled
description: The response enables the legacy XSS auditor with `X-XSS-Protection: 1` or `1; mode=block`. The auditor was removed from current browsers, and where it still runs it can be abused to suppress or alter parts of a page, so enabling it is at best inert and at worst harmful.
remediation: Send `X-XSS-Protection: 0` or omit the header, and rely on a Content-Security-Policy for script control.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the enabling value; it does not evaluate whether a legacy engine is in use and cannot show the auditor acting on a page.
scopeT: One response whose X-XSS-Protection value enables the auditor.
fp: A value of 0 is not reported; it is the recommended setting.
recordDesc: The XSS auditor this header enables is removed from current browsers, so the header is inert, and older engines that still honour it can be steered by crafted input.
applicability: Responses that send X-XSS-Protection.
risk: The header changes nothing in current browsers and in legacy engines can blank page sections; LOW because either outcome is limited.
why: The value is 1, with or without mode=block.
fix: Set X-XSS-Protection to 0 or remove it.
Rely on Content-Security-Policy instead.
verifyT: Fetch the page and confirm the header is 0 or absent.

title: X-UA-Compatible forces a legacy document mode
description: The response asks the browser to render in a legacy document mode through `X-UA-Compatible`. Current browsers ignore the header, and where it is still honoured it selects an older engine with weaker behaviour than the standards mode the page was tested in.
remediation: Remove X-UA-Compatible and serve standards mode. If an intranet client genuinely needs a legacy mode, scope the header to that deployment rather than to every response.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the header; it cannot tell which engine a given client selects or whether the page depends on legacy behaviour.
scopeT: One response whose X-UA-Compatible value selects a legacy document mode.
fp: A deployment that needs the header for a scoped intranet client is still reported; the finding is that it applies to this response.
recordDesc: X-UA-Compatible pins the rendering engine to a legacy mode that the current browsers no longer provide, so the header either does nothing or selects weaker behaviour.
applicability: Responses that send X-UA-Compatible.
risk: A legacy engine renders the page with older parsing and security behaviour, and the page is no longer what the developers tested; LOW because the header is inert in current browsers.
why: The response carries an X-UA-Compatible header naming an IE document mode.
fix: Remove X-UA-Compatible.
Serve standards mode.
verifyT: Fetch the page and confirm the header is absent.

title: Access-Control-Allow-Headers permits Authorization
description: The preflight response lists `Authorization` in Access-Control-Allow-Headers, so the browser will attach a bearer token or basic credential to the actual cross-origin request. Every origin the allow-list admits can therefore use the caller's credential against this endpoint.
remediation: Do not permit Authorization cross-origin unless a specific, small set of origins must send it. Keep the origin allow-list explicit and never reflect arbitrary origins beside a credential-bearing endpoint.
limitation: One header value. The rule reads the preflight allow-list and cannot see the request Origin, so it does not claim that any particular origin is admitted.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Headers value lists Authorization.
fp: A preflight that allows the header but answers a strict origin allow-list is still reported; the rule reports the header grant, not the origin decision.
recordDesc: Permitting Authorization in the preflight allow-list lets the browser send the caller credential cross-origin, so the origin allow-list now decides who may act with that credential.
applicability: Preflight responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Headers.
risk: An allow-listed origin reads authenticated data with the user token, and any origin reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin receives that capability; MEDIUM because the allow-list still has to admit the origin.
why: Access-Control-Allow-Headers names Authorization.
fix: Remove Authorization from the allow-list unless a fixed origin set needs it.
Keep the origin allow-list explicit.
verifyT: Send a preflight with Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization and confirm the response no longer allows it.

title: Access-Control-Allow-Methods permits TRACE
description: The preflight response advertises `TRACE` in Access-Control-Allow-Methods. TRACE echoes the request back, and allowing it cross-origin with credentials invites a cross-site tracing attempt against the endpoint; the method is also unnecessary for any JSON API.
remediation: Remove TRACE from Access-Control-Allow-Methods and disable the method at the server. Advertise only the verbs the API actually serves.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the advertised method and cannot show whether the server would answer a TRACE request.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Methods value lists TRACE.
fp: The HTTP Allow header is a different surface with its own rule.
recordDesc: Advertising TRACE in a CORS preflight makes the echo method reachable from an allowed origin, which is a known cross-site tracing primitive.
applicability: Preflight responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Methods.
risk: An allow-listed origin can send a credentialed TRACE request and read the echoed headers; LOW because the origin allow-list must still admit it and most servers disable TRACE.
why: Access-Control-Allow-Methods lists TRACE.
fix: Remove TRACE from the advertised methods.
Disable TRACE at the server.
verifyT: Send a preflight and confirm TRACE is no longer advertised; send TRACE and confirm it is refused.

title: Cache-Control declares public and no-store together
description: The Cache-Control header contains both `public` and `no-store`. The directives describe opposite intents: `no-store` says nothing may be written to a cache, while `public` says a shared cache may keep the response. Implementations differ in which they honour, so the actual caching of the response depends on the intermediary.
remediation: State one caching intent per response. For per-user data use `no-store`; for shareable content drop no-store and keep the freshness directives.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the contradictory pair and does not decide which directive an intermediary applies.
scopeT: One response whose Cache-Control value contains public and no-store.
fp: A response that uses private with no-store is not reported; the contradiction requires public.
recordDesc: Cache-Control declares public and no-store at the same time, so whether an intermediary stores the response depends on its directive precedence rather than on the deployment policy.
applicability: Responses that send Cache-Control.
risk: A shared cache that honours public may store a response the deployment meant to keep out of caches, which can expose per-user content; LOW because most caches give no-store precedence.
why: Cache-Control contains both public and no-store.
fix: State a single caching intent.
Use no-store alone for per-user data.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm Cache-Control carries either public or no-store, not both.

title: Expires header is not a valid HTTP date
description: The Expires header carries a value that is not an HTTP date, such as `0` or `-1`. A user agent cannot parse it, so the attribute is ignored and the freshness decision falls back to heuristic caching from the other headers, which usually gives the response a longer life than the deployment intended.
remediation: Send an HTTP date, or drop Expires and express the lifetime with Cache-Control max-age. Never use the legacy `0` or `-1` sentinels.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the date shape only; it does not compute the freshness lifetime a cache would derive.
scopeT: One response whose Expires value is not an HTTP date.
fp: A response with no Expires header is not reported; the rule needs the malformed value.
recordDesc: An Expires value that is not an HTTP date is ignored, so the response freshness falls back to heuristics instead of the declared lifetime.
applicability: Responses that send Expires.
risk: A response meant to expire immediately can be heuristically cached for a long period, which stale-serves per-user content; LOW because Cache-Control usually decides first.
why: Expires does not parse as an HTTP date.
fix: Send a valid HTTP date or remove Expires.
Express lifetime with Cache-Control max-age.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm Expires is a valid HTTP date or absent.

cells.safe: Expires carries an HTTP date or is absent

title: Multipart Content-Type omits the boundary parameter
description: The Content-Type declares a multipart media type without the `boundary` parameter. The boundary is what separates the parts, so a receiver cannot split the body and falls back to its own guessing or refuses the message; either way the declared type is not the type the receiver processes.
remediation: Send the boundary parameter with the multipart type and keep it unpredictable. Where the body is not multipart, use the type that describes it.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the parameter only; it does not parse the body and cannot show how a particular client handles the missing parameter.
scopeT: One response whose multipart Content-Type omits the boundary parameter.
fp: A missing Content-Type header is a different finding with its own rule.
recordDesc: A multipart Content-Type without a boundary cannot be parsed as declared, so the receiver guesses or rejects the body instead of reading the parts the sender wrote.
applicability: Responses that send a multipart Content-Type.
risk: A client that guesses the boundary can be steered into reading attacker-chosen part boundaries, and a strict client refuses the response; LOW because the affected content is multipart bodies rather than scripts.
why: Content-Type is multipart/* with no boundary parameter.
fix: Add the boundary parameter.
Use a type that matches the body.
verifyT: Fetch the response and confirm the multipart type carries a boundary.
